nodes.question: What are the major thematic lines addressed in the thematic collection of Topoi regarding the crisis of knowledge?
nodes.answer: The major thematic lines include the quantity, quality, and nature of information that circulates, the creation and dissemination of information and how it affects specific targets, and the normative consequences of the current knowledge crisis for individuals and institutions.
nodes.paragraph: It contains a series of papers all previously selected through a double-blind peer-review process presented at an international workshop with the same title, held in Milan on September 11 and 12, 2023, at the University Vita-Salute San Raffaele, and organized by the European Centre for Social Ethics (ECSE). The articles in this volume revolve around several major thematic lines. The first concerns the quantity, quality, and nature of the information that circulates, especially on the Internet, and from which socially relevant and sometimes dangerous phenomena emerge, as they can influence indi - vidual decisions. The second addresses the way in which information is created and disseminated and how it ulti - mately reaches specific targets. The third part deals with the normative consequences of the current knowledge crisis scenario for both individuals and institutions. In The Political and Socio-Epistemic Risks of Quanti - fication, Luca Ausili reflects on the growing tendency of political leaders to make use of empirical data to quantify information in an attempt to convey objectivity and rational - ity qualities inherently associated with numbers. Express - ing themselves through the use of quantified data betrays political leaders need to make the information they com - municate appear unbiased and impersonal.

nodes.question: What are the major thematic lines explored in the thematic collection "The Crisis of Knowledge: Ethics, Politics, Epistemology"?
nodes.answer: The major thematic lines include the quantity, quality, and nature of information circulating, how information is created and disseminated, and the normative consequences of the current knowledge crisis for individuals and institutions.
nodes.paragraph: But, as Ausili argues, the assumption that numbers are truly an expression of neutrality and impersonality is simply wrong, and this pursuit of quantification at all costs carries significant politi - cal risks. First, not all numerical data are necessarily objec - tive: data can be derived and also read in different ways, and not necessarily objectively. Secondly, this pursuit of quanti - fication at all costs carries the risk that anything that cannot be quantified and cannot be directly translated into a num - ber will be excluded from the political debate. This runs the risk of ignoring the needs and problems of the population and creating disillusionment and distrust of political leaders who seem to systematically ignore anything that cannot be expressed in numbers. Aaron Ben-ze ev , in his article The Crisis of Roman - tic Knowledge: The Role of Information and Ignorance in Times of Romantic Abundance, reflects on how the abun - dance of personal information shared and transmitted on digital dating platforms makes it harder to form solid and lasting romantic relationships. Having so many details about a potential partner does not necessarily make it easier to start a relationship, nor does it increase happiness; instead, the simpler rule of thumb seems to be much more effective in this regard.

nodes.question: What are some major thematic lines addressed in the thematic collection of Topoi regarding the crisis of knowledge?
nodes.answer: The thematic lines include the quantity, quality, and nature of circulating information, the creation and dissemination of information, and the normative consequences of the knowledge crisis for individuals and institutions.
nodes.paragraph: Relying entirely on information when choos - ing a partner leaves out an essential component of dating choices: intuition. The research presented in the paper Evaluating Intel - ligence and Knowledge in Large Language Models by Francesco Bianchini addresses a different issue. Large language models (LLMs) are generative models of artifi - cial intelligence that are able to produce natural language texts in response to human prompts that are almost indis - tinguishable from human-generated texts. Do LMMs pro - mote or hinder knowledge? What are the potential risks to their users? The first issue discussed concerns the immense proliferation of Al-generated texts on the Internet texts that, because of their artificial nature, are not perceived as a source of knowledge, which could end up pushing indi - viduals to retreat into ignorance. Indeed, at some point, ignorance may be perceived as a refuge in the face of the advancement of these technologies, which mimic human intelligence almost perfectly. A second problem relates to the manipulability of LLMs: these systems answer ques - tions posed by humans and can generate completely ficti - tious content.

nodes.question: What are some of the main thematic lines discussed in the thematic collection of Topoi concerning the crisis of knowledge?
nodes.answer: The main thematic lines include the quantity, quality, and nature of information circulating, the creation and dissemination of information, and the normative consequences of the knowledge crisis for individuals and institutions.
nodes.paragraph: LLMs simulate human reasoning, but they do not reason; rather, they make predictions based on the input or data they receive, which can be fabricated ad hoc. These risks highlight the need for the users of LLMs to develop a greater awareness of how LLMs work so that they can reap the benefits derived from these systems, which, if used well, can undoubtedly promote knowledge creation. In Algorithmic Objectivity as Ideology. Toward a Criti - cal Ethics of Digital Capitalism, Giuseppe De Ruvo illus - trates the limits of algorithmic implementation and raises questions about their only supposed objectivity. First, the paper questions what an algorithm is, which it defines as an abstract machine consisting of a complex set of impera - tive, defined, finite rules that must perform a specific cal - culation efficiently. But what does an algorithm actually do? Algorithms perform calculations, and those calcula - tions also involve making predictions. The more complex the contexts, the less accurate and realistic the calculations performed by algorithms can be, even though they are pre - sented as tools that produce objective results and cannot make mistakes.
